title: From Predictor to Assistant
objective: After this level you can explain how pretraining on vast amounts of text, then fine-tuning with human feedback, turns a text predictor into a chatbot.
summary: Next-token prediction isn't instruction-following. Fine-tuning on human-written answers, then RLHF with a reward model trained on rankings, turns a predictor into an assistant.

cards.headline: Trained on the internet, a model learns to continue text, not to help.
cards.body: A model pretrained on vast amounts of text is very good at one thing: predicting the next token. But predicting what comes next on a web page is a different goal from following your instructions helpfully and safely, as a 2022 paper pointed out. Turning one into the other took people.

cards.headline: Step 1: show it good answers
cards.body: Pretraining gives the model its raw skill with language. Then people write example answers to real prompts, showing the behavior they want, and the model is fine-tuned on those demonstrations. It's the same nudging of weights as Level 83, now aimed at answering like a helpful assistant instead of continuing a web page.

cards.headline: Step 2: rank, reward, repeat
cards.body: Writing perfect answers is slow, so labelers do something quicker: they rank several of the model's answers from best to worst. A second model, the reward model, learns from those rankings to score any answer by how much people would likely prefer it. The chatbot is then tuned to earn higher scores. That's reinforcement learning from human feedback, or RLHF.

cards.fact: A tuned model with 100 times fewer parameters beat the untuned giant.
cards.context: In the 2022 tests, people preferred answers from a 1.3 billion-parameter tuned model to those of the 175 billion-parameter GPT-3. The authors added a caveat: the labelers were a team of 40 contractors, so the model was aligned to a specific group, not to any broader notion of human values.

questions.prompt: In reinforcement learning from human feedback, what do the human labelers mainly do?

options.label: Write the model's code line by line
options.rationale: The model's behavior is tuned, not coded.

options.label: Rank several of the model's answers from best to worst
Type out every answer the chatbot will ever give
options.rationale: Rankings train a reward model that scores new answers.

options.label: Count the tokens in each answer

questions.explanation: Labelers rank model answers; a reward model learns from the rankings and the chatbot is tuned to score higher.

questions.prompt: People preferred a tuned 1.3 billion-parameter model over the 175 billion-parameter GPT-3. Which explanation fits best?

options.label: Smaller models always know more than bigger ones
options.rationale: The 2022 study credits the tuning, not the size.

options.label: The small model simply copied the big one's best answers
options.rationale: It was fine-tuned with human feedback, not copied.

options.label: Human-feedback tuning aimed it at following instructions
The big model had never been trained at all
options.rationale: GPT-3 was fully pretrained; it just wasn't tuned to follow instructions.

questions.explanation: Next-token prediction is a different goal from following instructions; human feedback tuned the small model toward that goal.

questions.prompt: Level 1 said software is instructions that tell hardware what to do. Where does a chatbot's helpful answering style mostly come from?

options.label: A programmer wrote an instruction for every possible question
options.rationale: The style was learned from people's example answers and rankings.

options.label: The processor's clock speed
options.rationale: Speed doesn't decide how an answer is worded.

options.label: The chatbot voting on its own answers
options.rationale: People did the ranking; a reward model learned from them.

options.label: Tuning on people's example answers and rankings

questions.explanation: The hardware still follows instructions, but the helpful style was learned by fine-tuning on human demonstrations and rankings.
